segments.text: Hello and welcome to the last lecture in our introduction to photonics video series.
This is going to be our last lecture, and in a sense is a segue to other courses in this online curriculum.
We started playing with lasers, and as you acquired certain skills in photonics,
you will be exposed to lasers that have a higher power,
so the whole issue of laser safety starts playing an important role.
In the last lecture we talked about anatomy of a human eye,
and we've seen that laser power, power from the lasers, poses a hazard to the safety of the human eye.
So this lecture, lecture number eight, or the last lecture in this video series,
is going to be dedicated to the lasers and the laser safety.
So in this lecture we are going to describe the laser classifications based on certain standards established by authorities.
We are going to define a concept called maximum permissible exposure,
a concept that plays an important role in laser safety.
We are going to talk about three general types of laser hazard controls.
We'll mention and show a few warning signs that are used to indicate the laser safety hazards.
We are also going to address the most frequent causes of laser accidents
and finally we are going to talk about laser safety precautions that you as photonics technicians
should take into account when you're working with lasers.
So the need to address this issue has been established already back in the 70s,
so the last century when lasers had been invented and started being used.
And the first standard that has been established is back in 1969.
It's been established at the request of the U.S. Department of Labor and addressed the issue of the laser safety.
This original laser safety standard has been updated a few times since present time.
For example, in 1973 another standard has been established and directed primarily to users
such as operators, technicians, laser safety officers, safety engineers, and research personnel.
And then there has been a few more updates in 1980, 1986, 1993.
There was a revision back in 2000.
So as lasers are evolving, as lasers are being developed,
so do the laser safety standards that are being evolved to address specific issues
that are related to the new developments in the whole area of laser safety.
So the primary laser safety standard for the industry is so-called NCZ136.1.
And then there's also a specific type of laser safety standard for educational institutions,
so-called NCA136.5.
These standards can be obtained by different institutions,
specifically the Laser Institute of America that's been stationed in Orlando, Florida,
and can give you access to this type of documents.
And also they may be available also online.
You can purchase these documents that are having a pretty large number of pages
that you would have to read, especially if you are to be a certified
as a laser safety officer or a person who's going to be responsible
for the safety in a photonics or laser labs.
You will have to read it through these documents and you will have to study
in detail all the aspects of laser safety.
So according to laser safety standards, lasers are classified into a few groups
based on the potential hazards that they pose.
So we are going to start with the class I, so-called exempt lasers.
This type of lasers, this class of lasers cannot, under normal operating conditions,
emit a hazardous level of optical radiation.
And the lasers that are included in this category is certain lasers
that are part of the laboratory equipment with all beam paths
and reflections that are enclosed.
So you may have other lasers of a higher class, like class IV or class III,
that can be classified as a class I
if there's a proper enclosure that has been put around that type of a laser.
The next in the list of classifications of lasers is so-called class II.
Here we are talking about low power visible laser devices of about 1 milliwatt.
So these types of lasers would not have enough output power to injure a person
accidentally, but may injure the eye if it stayed for a long period of time.
So that's another important aspect that has to be mentioned.
So it's not just about the power or irradiance of the laser.
It's also about exposure time.
So you will see that you have to take into account
both the power of the laser and exposure time in order to properly quantify
whether a laser is posing any kind of threat or risk for laser safety.
So back to class number II.
Class II usually is going to be labeled with a caution sign
that has to be put on a device.
Types of lasers that would go under the class II would be many helium neon lasers,
not all of them.
And these types of lasers are usually used for alignment procedures and optical experiments.
So if you have a higher power type of a laser,
you don't want to fool around with that type of laser during the alignment procedure.
So the way how you're aligning a higher class laser
is basically having another laser that's part of the same laser enclosure
that's visible and that's classified as class II, which doesn't pose the risk.
So you're going to do the whole alignment procedure.
You're going to align the beam of the class II laser,
and then you're going to turn off that laser
and then turn on the high power laser of class III or class IV.
That's going to be the main laser for your experiment.
Next class is class IIIa.
Here we are talking about power levels of 1 milliwatt up to 5 milliwatts.
These types of lasers cannot injure a normal person
when viewed with an unaided eye,
but may cause injury when energy is collected
and put into the eye using certain focusing optics,
such as binoculars, etc.
So in this class, most laser pointers will be classified,
and in this case, you would want to put a danger or caution sign
on the device depending on the irradiance,
depending on the amount of power that that laser is going to radiate.
Next class is class IIIb.
Here we start getting serious in terms of the laser safety.
We're talking about power levels from 5 milliwatts to 500 milliwatt.
These lasers can produce eye injury when viewed without eye protection.
So if you are experimenting, if you're working with class IIIb and class IV lasers,
you have to wear laser eye protection at all times.
So this class of laser would require a danger label
and could have a dangerous specular reflection,
meaning not only that this laser poses the safety risk
if your eyes are exposed directly to the laser beam,
so if laser beam is directed towards the certain reflecting surface
that can reflect the laser beam,
especially specular reflections or reflections
that are not being scattered or diffused in many directions.
So as already mentioned, if you are working with class IIIb laser,
you have to wear the eye protection at all times.
And finally, the highest class is class IV.
We are talking about lasers that have powers above half a watt
or above 500 milliwatts.
These types of lasers can injure you if viewed directly
or by viewing both the specular or diffused reflections.
So here it's not just the specular but also diffused reflections.
The engine side has to label this type of a laser
and some of these lasers can also present a tire hazard.
And in this case, both eye and skin protection
would be required in operating this type of a laser.
So as this slide shows, lasers, according to laser safety standards,
are going to be classified in different classes starting with class I
and going all the way to class IV
from the lowest possible power levels
all the way to the highest possible power levels.

what type of safety controls would have to be established

class III and class IV type of lasers.

that operate at the power levels above half a watt.

you definitely have to have a very explicitly defined
type of laser safety controls in the lab
that would prevent any kind of injuries to your eye and to your skin.
There's a few different types of control measures
according to the laser safety standards.
Control measures can be broken down into three main types.
You may establish engineering controls.
You may have administrative controls.
And finally, you may wear personal protected equipment
or popularly known as PPE.
So when we are talking about engineering controls,
we are talking about certain design features or devices.
So we are talking about hardware in this case.

to the laser, laser beam or laser environment,
that would restrict exposure or reduce irradiance.
So what kind of controls are we talking about here?
We're talking about beam shutters.
We're talking about beam attenuators,
remote firing and monitoring systems,
and also protective housing placed entirely around some laser systems.
So very often, laser labs would have interlocks.
The doors would be carefully controlled.
There would have to be some sort of laser sign,
laser safety light outside that would be turned on
during the operation of the laser.
And if someone opens the door during the laser operation,
there would have to be some sort of automatic shutdown of the laser.
So we are talking about a lot of hardware
that would be used to reduce any kind of risk of laser safety,
of laser injury during the operation of the laser.
Not only are we talking about monitoring systems,
we're also talking about certain features,

You know, you may have a beam dumps

So a lot of different types of engineering controls
that can be established in the laser lab.
Next, a group is so-called administrative control measures.
Here we are talking about certain procedures.
We are talking about the information,
rather than devices and mechanical systems.
So important administrative controls
would be posting warning signs and labels,
establishment of SOPs or standard operating procedures,
safety training.
Very often people who are entering the lab
would have to sign in with a specific date and time
when they entered the lab,
and they also have to sign out when they are leaving the lab.
Very often those types of laser safety books
or operating books in the labs
would also include different measurements
or experiments that have been conducted in the laser lab.
So a lot of paperwork that we're talking about here,
so we're talking about administrative control measures
that can be established in a laser lab.
And finally, the third group of safety controls
is so-called PPE, or personal protective equipment.
So here we are talking about equipment
that is worn by the personnel,
such as laser technicians, laser safety officers,
and other people who will be present in a laser lab.
So we're talking about protective eyewear,
we're talking about gloves,
we're talking about special clothing,
so anything that can go on an operator
or on a human being that is present in a laser lab
is what's going to go
under the personal protective equipment.
This slide shows in a form of a table
the classifications of different types of safety controls
listed in three columns.

An important concept that has to be introduced
